items.q: **(Sommerville Ch1)** Why is professional software *not* simply the programs that have been developed?
options: Because programs are always written in C
Because it also includes the associated documentation, configuration data and libraries needed to operate it correctly
Because professional software has no source code
Because it must always be open-source
items.explain: Sommerville Ch1: professional software is developed by teams for use by others and is more than the program — it includes documentation, configuration data and supporting libraries/data files required to make the program work correctly.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch1, exercise)** Which set lists the *four important attributes* all professional software should have?
items.explain: Sommerville Ch1 names exactly these four essential attributes of good software: maintainability, dependability & security, efficiency, and acceptability.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch1)** Which is a fundamental principle of *professional & ethical responsibility* for software engineers?
options: Maximise personal profit on every project
Respect the confidentiality of employers/clients and only accept work within your competence
Always use the newest programming language
items.explain: Sommerville Ch1 lists professional responsibilities: confidentiality, competence (don't misrepresent your skill / accept work beyond it), intellectual-property rights, and not misusing computers. SE is more than technical skill.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch2, exercise)** For a safety-critical system to control the *anti-lock braking* in a car, which process model is most appropriate, and why?
options: A plan-driven waterfall-style model, because requirements are stable and rigorous documentation/verification are essential
items.explain: Sommerville Ch2 reasoning: braking control has stable, well-understood, safety-critical requirements demanding extensive verification and documentation — a plan-driven (waterfall-like) approach fits, not agile.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch2)** A stated *disadvantage* of incremental development (compared to waterfall) is that:
options: It cannot deliver working software early
System structure tends to degrade as new increments are added, and the process is less visible
items.explain: Sommerville Ch2: incremental development reduces change cost and gives early delivery/feedback, BUT the process is less visible (fewer documents) and system structure degrades unless effort is spent on refactoring.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch2)** In the spiral model, what happens in every loop that distinguishes it from other models?
options: Risks are explicitly identified, analysed and resolved before proceeding
The customer signs a fixed-price contract
All code is rewritten from scratch
items.explain: Sommerville Ch2 (Boehm's spiral): each loop = objective setting → risk assessment & reduction → development & validation → planning. Explicit, continuous risk management is its defining trait.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch3)** Which is one of the core *principles of agile methods*?
options: Customer involvement and incremental delivery, with people — not process — driving development and embracing change
items.explain: Sommerville Ch3 lists agile principles: customer involvement, incremental delivery, people not process, embrace change, and maintain simplicity.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch3)** A key problem when applying agile methods to *large, long-lifetime* systems is:
options: Informal, minimal documentation and the need for up-front architecture/contracts can make scaling and long-term maintenance difficult
Agile is illegal for large systems
items.explain: Sommerville Ch3: agile suits small/medium co-located teams; for large systems its light documentation, distributed teams, fixed-price contracts and the need for some up-front design create scaling challenges.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch3 / Pressman, XP)** In XP, the practice of *pair programming* primarily provides:
options: Continuous, informal code review and shared knowledge/ownership of the code
items.explain: XP pair programming = two developers at one machine; it gives continuous review, spreads knowledge (collective ownership) and tends to improve quality, at the cost of more developer-hours.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch4, exercise)** A frequently cited *problem of using natural language* to specify requirements is:
options: Ambiguity, over-flexibility and lack of modularisation make requirements easy to misinterpret
It cannot be read by stakeholders
It is illegal under IEEE standards
items.explain: Sommerville Ch4: natural-language requirements suffer ambiguity (multiple readings), over-flexibility (same thing said many ways) and poor modularisation — hence structured forms, tables and models are added.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch4)** The requirements engineering process is usually described by which four activities?
options: Elicitation, analysis, specification and validation (plus management)
items.explain: Sommerville Ch4 structures RE as elicitation & analysis, specification, and validation, with requirements management running across the project.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch4)** Which best states the difference between functional and non-functional requirements?
options: FRs are about performance; NFRs are about features
FRs state services/behaviour the system must provide; NFRs are constraints on those services (e.g. timing, reliability, standards)
FRs are written by users; NFRs are written by lawyers
items.explain: Sommerville Ch4: functional requirements describe what the system should do (services, reactions); non-functional requirements are constraints/qualities on those services and often apply to the system as a whole.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch4)** In Sommerville's NFR classification, *regulatory, ethical and legislative* requirements fall under which type?
items.explain: Sommerville Ch4 NFR taxonomy: Product (runtime behaviour), Organisational (org policies/standards), and External (factors outside the system/org — regulatory, ethical, legislative).

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch4)** Why should non-functional requirements be expressed *quantitatively* using a metric?
options: So they are objectively *verifiable* — vague goals like 'easy to use' cannot be tested
To hide the requirement from developers
items.explain: Sommerville Ch4 gives a metrics table (speed→transactions/sec, reliability→MTTF, ease of use→training time, etc.) precisely so NFRs become measurable and testable rather than vague goals.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch4)** During requirements *validation*, the check that asks 'can the requirements actually be implemented within budget and technology?' is the:
items.explain: Sommerville Ch4 validation checks: validity, consistency, completeness, realism (implementable with available budget/technology) and verifiability.

items.q: **(Pressman, requirements modelling)** A use case primarily describes:
options: A sequence of interactions between an actor and the system to achieve a goal
items.explain: Pressman: a use case is a scenario describing how an actor (role) interacts with the system to accomplish a goal, including the main success scenario and alternative/exception flows.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch8)** What is the essential difference between *verification* and *validation*?
options: Verification checks the software conforms to its specification; validation checks it meets the customer's real needs
Verification is done by customers; validation by developers
Verification needs no execution; validation forbids reviews
items.explain: Sommerville Ch8 (Boehm): verification = 'are we building the product right?' (vs specification); validation = 'are we building the right product?' (vs user needs).

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch8)** Sommerville describes development testing as having which stages?
options: Unit testing, component (integration) testing, and system testing
items.explain: Sommerville Ch8 'development testing' = unit testing (individual units), component testing (integrated units/interfaces), and system testing (the whole system). Release & user testing follow.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch8 / Pressman)** In test-driven development (TDD), the correct order is:
options: Write a failing test → write minimal code to pass it → refactor
Write all tests at the end → ship
items.explain: TDD cycle (red-green-refactor): write a failing test first, write just enough code to pass, then refactor. Benefits: code coverage, regression safety, and clearer requirements.

items.q: **(Pressman, black-box testing)** Equivalence partitioning and boundary-value analysis are techniques for:
options: Black-box (functional) testing — choosing inputs from the specification without seeing the code
items.explain: Pressman: equivalence partitioning (divide inputs into classes) and boundary-value analysis (test at the edges) are black-box techniques derived from the specification, not the code structure.
